title: The unseen
hook: believing in what isn't seen is where faith starts (2:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the angels, and your line: the ones who write. Did you hand them one good intention? Angels are part of something larger the Qur'an names right at its start. Day six hundred sixty-six.

A short list of things you trusted today without seeing them. The signal that carried your messages. The pilot of a plane you heard overhead. The person who cooked food you bought. The air in the room, which you breathed several hundred times and never once looked at. Trust in what you can't see isn't strange. Nobody gets through a Tuesday without it. And when the Qur'an describes the people it's meant for, on its second page, the very first quality it names is exactly that.

Al-Baqarah begins by calling the book a guidance for those who keep their duty, and then describes them. Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, starts: "Who believe in the Unseen." Before prayer, before giving, before anything they do, the first thing named is what they trust. The Arabic is al-ghayb. The root gh-y-b means to be absent, hidden from view. A student who misses class is gha'ib, absent. So the unseen isn't the imaginary. It's what is real but not in front of you. What's in it? A well-known hadith in Sahih Muslim, where Jibril comes as a stranger and questions the Prophet, lists the heart of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the measuring out of good and bad. Almost all of it sits in the unseen. And the Qur'an is honest about who holds it. In surah six it says that with Allah are the keys of the unseen, and no one knows them but Him. It adds a small, startling picture: not a leaf falls but He knows it. Surah twenty-seven says no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah. That's why classical scholars were firm about fortune-tellers: a hadith in Sahih Muslim warns that whoever consults one to ask about hidden things has their prayer unaccepted for forty nights. Faith in the unseen, then, has two sides. It trusts what can't be seen. And it doesn't pretend to see it. The future, the hidden, the leaf before it falls: those stay with Allah.
screen: `TRUST IT, DON'T CLAIM TO SEE IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trust one unseen thing. Sit still and close your eyes, so the seen goes quiet. Feel your breath coming in. You can't see the air, but you're living on it. Feel your heart, if you can find it, doing its work without your watching. Now pick one unseen thing to rest your weight on for the rest of this sit. It might be your breath, someone's love for you, or, if you believe, Allah's care. Don't try to picture it. Just lean on it. The bell holds the time.
The unseen. Al-ghayb, from gh-y-b, absent: what is real but out of view, the first thing named in al-Baqarah's picture of faith. Today's word.
Your line: faith in the unseen. Today, when you catch yourself guessing the future, let one guess go and leave it with the one who holds the keys. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims describe faith (iman) as belief in Allah, the angels, the revealed books, the messengers, the Last Day and divine decree, much of it in the unseen; classical scholars warned against fortune-telling as a claim on what only Allah knows.

original.note: Arabic: the unseen, from gh-y-b, to be absent.

trapdoor: what you thought: the unseen means ghosts and mysteries.
what it means: al-ghayb is what is real but out of view, and faith begins by trusting it (2:3).
what a scholar hears: gh-y-b is the root of gha'ib, absent; the Qur'an keeps its keys with Allah alone (6:59; 27:65).
